Crude Oil - Call to Ban Palm Oil

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We examine the impact of a product that has decimated huge tracts of virgin forest in south east Asia and ask "is there merit to calls to ban Palm Oil?"

Unique Selling Point:
Social media is driving a growing international campaign to ban Palm Oil because of its devastating impact on forest biodiversity, including endangered species like the Orangutan. It's a vegetable oil that is found in a range of products from ice-creams to pies and mascara. The industry has responded to the mounting criticism by establishing a body that certifies sustainable Palm Oil, but that hasn't satisfied some lobbyists. They say rogue suppliers continue to operate, and that the certified standards are too vague. All of which makes for an unsurprising stand-off between environmentalists and big business.

But, this is a complex issue and, sadly, the debate rarely takes that into account. Ours aims to be a more nuanced insert that explains the impact of Palm Oil, takes a closer look at attempts to re-package the industry as one committed to sustainability and the efforts of rogue suppliers to prioritise profits over the environment.

Summary:
Cultivating Palm Oil makes economic sense. It's 10 times more productive than soya, and does just about everything you demand of a tasteless vegetable oil. Ironically, it also makes environmental sense because - given its outstanding yields - you need less land to produce more oil than would be the case with other species. But, here's the rub: it only makes environmental sense if you're not slashing-and-burning virgin forest to make way for more palm trees. If you do, not only are you creating more pollution and destroying a vital carbon sink, you're decimating the habitat of dozens of animals including tigers, monkeys and orangutans.

For a very long time, that's precisely what happened. Swathes of forest were cleared in Malaysia and Indonesia in particular as the global demand for Palm Oil continued to rocket. The result was a massive pay-day for the suppliers and millers, and social and environmental misery for just about everybody else.

Thanks to the efforts of international organisations like Mighty Earth, the industry was pressured into adopting measures aimed at limiting its environmental impact, including a pledge not to chop down any more forests. That, for some, has been enough: many suppliers peg their reputations on this certification process and consumers who care about such things are able to buy guilt-free butter and hair gel. For others, though, it's a charade. They argue that forests continue to burn, animals continue to die and local villagers continue to be fleeced of their land.

Leaning on the experience of international campaigners, we look into the local Palm Oil supply chain to gauge its commitment to sustainability and ask whether we as consumers can trust the certification process or whether what we're buying is the fruit of a now devastated landscape.

Script:


Carte Blanche: Palm Oil Script 2.

VO: Glenn Hurowitz has the walk of a man on a mission – and that’s because he is.

VO: He’s the Chief Executive of Mighty Earth – a campaign organisation with a reputation as a no-nonsense defender of the environment.

VO: A reputation regularly put to the test when nature and big business clash. As they do in South East Asia.

VO: This used to be pristine Indonesian rain forest, now reduced to a smouldering wasteland.

VO: Deforestation has been particularly devastating in Indonesia and Malaysia. And, while it has many causes, in these two countries one culprit stands out: Palm Oil.

ITV Glen Hurowitz STRAP “CEO: Mighty Earth” [00:00:27] Fifty thousand square kilometres of rainforest have been wiped off the face of the earth to make room for palm oil plantations.

VO: If that figure is hard to get your head around, perhaps another better illustrates the point:

ITV Glen Hurowitz [00:00:27] We've lost more than one hundred thousand orangutans over the last 25 years.

VO: It’s early 2016, in the aftermath of an intense dry spell in South East Asia, and a team from the organisation, International Animal Rescue, is at work.

VO: Close to starving, a female Orangutan fights the effects of anaesthetic darts. She was driven here by a fire that destroyed her habitat - something easily blamed on the drought. But this is Palm Oil country where fires are often deliberately set to make it easier to clear the trees.

VO: This, it turns out, is a double rescue. Safely on the ground, mother and baby are checked over by vets. They call her Mama Nam – she’s so malnourished she’s no longer producing milk.

LINK It’s footage like that which prompted our own closer look at Palm Oil, and there are many questions: what exactly is Palm Oil? If it is so destructive why do companies still manufacture it? And, if the destruction continues what will the impact be on the rain forests? What you might think is a simple case of good v evil, or money v the environment is lot more complex than that.

VO: First, the easy part: why so popular? Well, because it’s so versatile: Palm Oil is found in as much as half of everything we consume in our daily lives – it makes soap foamy, chocolate and coffee creamer creamy, biscuits crunchy and… well, you get the picture.

VO: That versatility and our hunger for healthier, cheaper vegetable oil explain the numbers: in 1995, around 15 million tonnes of Palm Oil was produced around the world. In just 23 years that’s jumped to 70 million tonnes and by 2050 production could more than triple.

VO: Small wonder then that vast tracts now look like this – about 13 million hectares in Indonesia alone.

ITV Victorine Che Thoner [17:40:09] Deforestation is that strong thing which is most undesirable. But then it is not only deforestation. There is child labour. There is land being taken away without free prior informed consent from local and indigenous communities.

VO: Victorine Che Thoner (Share-Torner) is a project leader at environmental NGO, Greenpeace.

ITV Victorine Che Thoner STRAP “Congo Basin Forest Campaign: Greenpeace Africa” [17:18:10] So you’re looking at climate change which is coming as a result of the deforestation which is going on. But you are also looking at this culture, this identity which is being lost as an impact as well.

VO: Work by NGO’s like Greenpeace and Mighty Earth to expose these abuses has led to calls for the Palm Industry to clean up its act – but just how much has been achieved?

LINK: Of the more than 70 million metric tonnes of Palm Oil produced every year, only about 20% is certified sustainable. The remaining 80% is made up of about 56 million metric tonnes of well… who knows what exactly?

VO: That 80%, called Conventional Palm Oil, is a mixture of sustainable and unsustainable product – a cocktail of often mysterious origins where much of the industry’s deforestation lurks. But, for now, let’s focus on the remaining 20% - the portion that’s certified as sustainable.

VO: We needed a picture of the local market, so we contacted several companies to ask whether they sourced their Palm Oil sustainably. The replies made for interesting reading.

LINK Not everyone we contacted took the time to get back to us, and the responses that we did receive ranged from the sublime to the ridiculous. Here’s an example of the latter from a cooking oil company: “we don’t ask for certification from our suppliers, therefore can’t take part in your survey”. Go figure.

VO: Clearly, not everyone’s committed to sustainability, but those keen to show us their environmental credentials are all flying the same flag.

VO: That of the RSPO - the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil. It’s a voluntary organisation of 4000 producers, traders and brands who meet certain criteria in order to have their products certified as sustainable – that magic 20%. A total ban on deforestation is one of them. Sounds good, right? Unfortunately, it’s not that simple.

VO: In its response, Woolworths said that an estimated “97% of all private label food lines and 72% of all private label beauty lines containing palm oil are sourcing RSPO (MB) palm oil. So far, so good. It continues… “and 50% in foods and 22% in beauty is so far certified as sustainable through supply chain audits.”

VO: Notice the discrepancy? Well, it’s because the sustainability of the supply chains behind the products need to be independently verified. In Woolies’ case, many are yet to go through that process.

VO: You might also have noticed the MB in the Woolworth’s statement. That refers to something called Mass Balance. It basically means certified sustainable oil is combined with conventional oil and labelled as something called “mixed”. The bulk of the products contain oil from this “mixed” category.
But certification is not where the complexity begins and ends, and that is best left to the industry to explain.

VO: Mark Wong is from Sime Darby Oils. A multi-national, they have a refinery in Gauteng but he’s flown in from the Netherlands to talk to us.

ITV Mark Wong STRAP “Head Downstream Sustainability, Sime Darby Oils” [00:03:20] roughly about 20 percent of global palm oil supply is certified to RSPO only half of that's really being bought as sustainable palm oil today.

VO: In other words, 20% is being produced, but 20% isn’t being sold.

VO: Our stones can help here: this is the “magic 20%”. Only half of that is going to the market as sustainable Palm Oil. And, as Mass Balance has shown, even that portion – the remaining 10% - has different levels of sustainability.

ITV: Mark Wong [00:07:31] at the heart of it it's really about that market mechanism (CUT) if you were to produce sustainable palm oil, there would be a market out there that would that would absorb that and it would help you to cover the costs of doing all these extra things. [00:25:32] everybody wants sustainable palm oil. But at no additional cost

VO: And that reluctance to pay has implications.

ITV Glen Hurowitz [00:12:38] one of the distressing things is that there's evidence that despite all of the attention to forests over the last 20 years, in many places deforestation rates have gone up.

VO: That’s partly because rogue Palm Oil companies – so-called dirty producers – continue to feed the system.

ITV Glen Hurowitz [[00:05:25] the number of rogue actors is down to say 20 but those 20 companies can do a lot of deforestation and we're seeing plantations that are 20000 hectares in size still being cleared

VO: And even certified sustainable Palm Oil isn’t always what it seems. In the dizzying network of plantations, mills, refineries, traders and customers that makes up this industry, dirty practises often hide behind clean brands.


ITV Victorine Che Thoner [17:21:46] So this kind of opaque structure makes it very difficult for you to be able to follow the supply chain and be able to say there is sustainability, there is no deforestation, there is no human rights abuse.


VO: A 2018 Greenpeace report exposed several of these companies. Worryingly, some were RSPO members but – more than that – they were linked to traders and global brands with very public anti-deforestation policies including Sime Darby.

ITV Mark Wong [00:23:32] What we're trying to do is we trying to get them to change their practices. Right.(CUT) If they stop clearing then there's no reason to actually kick them out the supply chain and punish them because you know they're actually showing that they're willing to go on this journey with us.

LINK Seems fair enough, right? Sime Darby is engaging with more than 30 suppliers who might be responsible for ongoing deforestation. But a closer look speaks volumes about the certification process and who is taking ultimate responsibility.

VO: This is Sime Darby’s so-called grievance list: it’s a compilation of 25 potential transgressors – many of them in the South African supply chain. But take a look at this column and you’ll see that it falls to donor-funded environmental groups like Mighty Earth and Greenpeace to do the detective work.

ITV Glen Hurowitz [00:08:05] We cannot rely over the long term on the mercies of billionaires to protect our natural resources. And therefore if we shifted our attention or people onto some other issue there's no guarantee that enforcement of those policies will continue.

ITV Victorine Che Thoner [17:30:45] these companies should not be waiting for someone to come and police them to be able to implement it. They create problems – they should also create the solutions and implement the solutions.

VO: If Sime Darby deserves credit, it’s for flagging close to a dozen other potentially rogue companies though its own, internal monitoring processes.

VO: So where does that leave you and me - the consumer? What role for us in this maze of bread, donuts, chips, biscuits and shampoo. Well, here’s the thing: according to at least one expert, there’s only so much we can do.

VO: The University of Cape Town’s Dr Shari Daya has unique insight into what’s known as sustainable consumption: what people are buying and why. And, apparently, middle class South Africans aren’t paying too much attention to Pam Oil.

ITV Shari Daya STRAP “Environmental& Geographical Sciences, UCT” AA060201.mp4
[00:01:48] (CUT) I think it takes time for these things to for that information to get out there and to settle into people to the point where they actually express it as a concern or they act on it as a concern.

VO: But, when or even if there is a backlash against unsustainable Palm Oil here, it might not be fair to expect consumers to lead the fightback.

ITV Shari Daya AA060301.mp4 [00:03:26] we all want to know what is in our food and how it is being produced and how it's being packaged, but expecting that information to translate into an overhaul of the food system is completely unrealistic.(CUT) AA060501.mp4 [00:00:29] I think the responsibility really needs to be shifted much more forcefully onto the actors who have the power to make change.

John [00:00:58] Who are?

ITV Shari Daya [00:00:59] Who are government our governments and the retailers, the corporations.

ITV Victorine Che Thoner (17:23:38) more pressure needs to come from consumer brands for these companies to straighten up. If they have no problem with their supply, or with the demand for their products, they will have no incentive to change
ENDS..

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We examine the impact of a product that has decimated huge tracts of virgin forest in south east Asia and ask "is there merit to calls to ban Palm Oil?"
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Social media is driving a growing international campaign to ban Palm Oil because of its devastating impact on forest biodiversity, including endangered species like the Orangutan. It's a vegetable oil that is found in a range of products from ice-creams to pies and mascara. The industry has responded to the mounting criticism by establishing a body that certifies sustainable Palm Oil, but that hasn't satisfied some lobbyists. They say rogue suppliers continue to operate, and that the certified standards are too vague. All of which makes for an unsurprising stand-off between environmentalists and big business. But, this is a complex issue and, sadly, the debate rarely takes that into account. Ours aims to be a more nuanced insert that explains the impact of Palm Oil, takes a closer look at attempts to re-package the industry as one committed to sustainability and the efforts of rogue suppliers to prioritise profits over the environment.
metadata.Summary: Cultivating Palm Oil makes economic sense. It's 10 times more productive than soya, and does just about everything you demand of a tasteless vegetable oil. Ironically, it also makes environmental sense because - given its outstanding yields - you need less land to produce more oil than would be the case with other species. But, here's the rub: it only makes environmental sense if you're not slashing-and-burning virgin forest to make way for more palm trees. If you do, not only are you creating more pollution and destroying a vital carbon sink, you're decimating the habitat of dozens of animals including tigers, monkeys and orangutans. For a very long time, that's precisely what happened. Swathes of forest were cleared in Malaysia and Indonesia in particular as the global demand for Palm Oil continued to rocket. The result was a massive pay-day for the suppliers and millers, and social and environmental misery for just about everybody else. Thanks to the efforts of international organisations like Mighty Earth, the industry was pressured into adopting measures aimed at limiting its environmental impact, including a pledge not to chop down any more forests. That, for some, has been enough: many suppliers peg their reputations on this certification process and consumers who care about such things are able to buy guilt-free butter and hair gel. For others, though, it's a charade. They argue that forests continue to burn, animals continue to die and local villagers continue to be fleeced of their land. Leaning on the experience of international campaigners, we look into the local Palm Oil supply chain to gauge its commitment to sustainability and ask whether we as consumers can trust the certification process or whether what we're buying is the fruit of a now devastated landscape.
